newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: PLDT seen meriting earnings upgrade.
newsitem.headline: PLDT seen meriting earnings upgrade.

text.p: Philippine Long Distance Telephone rang up a hefty 32 percent growth in net income in the first nine months of 1996, prompting analysts to consider upgrading their full-year profit targets.

The Philippines' dominant telecommunications provider reported on Wednesday that its nine-month net income rose to 4.693 billion pesos ($178 million) from 3.539 billion pesos ($135 million) over the same period in 1995.
The 1995 figure excludes a 1.154 billion peso ($44 million) extraordinary gain from the sale of part of its stake in mobile-phone subsidiary Pilipino Telephone Corp last year.
"The figure is above our expectations ... If PLDT continues with this trend, it will definitely overshoot our forecast," Bernadette Tamayo, investment analyst at BPI Capital Corp, told Reuters.
BPI had earlier forecast a 6.2 billion peso ($236 million) full-year 1996 profit for PLDT, slightly higher than the 5.751 billion pesos ($218 million) registered last year.
Erwin Tan, research head of Abacus Securities, said he expects Manila brokerages will raise their full-year targets by 5 to 10 percent.
Gina Dipaling, an analyst at Philippine Asian Equity Securities, said robust third-quarter earnings of around 1.75 billion pesos ($66 million) alone were reason enough for an upgrade.
"We will see a lot of upgrades in earnings for this year. Historically, the fourth quarter is the strongest in terms of turnover as well as net income," she said.

Philippine Asian Equity Securities had earlier forecast full-year net profit of 6.55 billion pesos ($249 million), well above the forecasts of other investment houses, which set it at around 6.0 billion pesos ($228 million).
The fourth-quarter figures are usually boosted by calls to home during Christmas by Filipinos living abroad.
"The company is returning to better quality earnings," said Ricardo Puig, senior analyst at Peregrine Securities.
Domestic calls are growing faster than international calls, whose rates are more vulnerable to adjustments and to foreign exchange fluctuations.
Revenues from long-distance calls of domestic origin grew 48.6 percent to 3.689 billion pesos ($140 million), while local-call revenues rose 25 percent to 5.285 billion pesos ($201 million).
The company attributed the growth to the installation of more lines. There were 1.36 million lines at the end of September, up 24.45 percent from 1.09 million in September 1995.
Analysts said savings from its employee redundancy programme had also complemented the higher operating revenues.
The company is expected to lay off an additional 600 to 700 workers this year to leave it with a total staff of 18,727 by the end of the year.
Dipaling said salaries, which used to account for 30 percent of its operating expenses, now accounted for only 28.7 percent.
Abacus's Tan said PLDT was strong enough to go on dominating the sector despite competition from new players and that its strong income growth will continue for two to three years.
PLDT shares rose 40 pesos ($1.50) to close at 1,585 pesos ($60.30) on Wednesday.
